PennSound

PennSound is an ongoing project committed to producing new audio recordings and preserving existing audio archives: a poetry website and online archive that hosts free, downloadable recordings of poets reading their own work, and of others' work. Its own YouTube channel calls it a Web-based archive for noncommercial distribution of the largest collection of poetry sound files on the Internet, and its Instagram account the world's preeminent online archive of poetry audio, with more than 50,000 recordings from 1913 to the present. It has been called the "iTunes for poetry", a phrase Wikipedia attributes to Charles Bernstein in an Associated Press article, and its running series of posts is PennSound Daily.

It is a project of the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing at the University of Pennsylvania, whose site lists it among the Center's programs beside the Kelly Writers House events and ModPo, under the Center's director, Al Filreis; PennSound itself is directed by Charles Bernstein, Filreis and Chris Mustazza and edited by Michael S. Hennessey, with Danny Snelson and Kenneth Goldsmith as senior editors. Two other descriptions name two directors: the description on its YouTube channel lists Bernstein and Filreis as directors, Hennessey as managing editor and Mark P. Lindsay as managing director, and a profile on poets.org, posted in December 2006, calls Bernstein one of the site's two directors along with Filreis. Filreis and Bernstein created it, and it was launched in 2005; an article on Penn Today under the title "PennSound: All the Free Poetry You Care to Download" opens by setting it against a recording industry that "may not want anyone downloading music without paying for it".

Recordings are filed on author pages, series pages, anthology, collection and group pages and in a singles archive, with Cinema, Classics, podcast and Close Listening collections and the PennSound Daily archive beside them. Readings are broken down into singles, one poem to a file, and complete readings are also kept; a 2006 profile set this organization against "many poetry audio archives", and newly segmented readings, cut by poem and by topic, continue to be announced. The PennSound Manifesto, by Bernstein, sets six rules, among them that recordings be free and downloadable and broken down into singles, that all files be named, that bibliographic information be embedded in each file, and that sound files be indexed and retrievable from a library catalog under the poet's name and from search engines on the web; the About page links it and the launch press release. The census records that a work is held under the poet's name on an author page and under a series name on series pages, such as Belladonna* and Love Jawns: A Mixtape, and that the saved pages state no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names. The archive's paper on heteronymy holds that a civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across the systems that govern scholarly, literary, institutional and platform production, copyright among them, and it distinguishes the pseudonym, which changes the label attached to an authorial function, from the heteronym, which changes the organization of the function itself.

Where the reader differs from the author, a recording names both: the historical selection on the home page lists John Clare's "Vowelless Letter" (1849) performed by Charles Bernstein, Hannah Weiner's Clairvoyant Journal performed by Weiner, Sharon Mattlin and Rochelle Kraut, Kurt Schwitters's "Ur Sonata: Largo" performed by Ernst Schwitters (spelled "Scwhitter" on the page), and Velimir Khlebnikov's "Incantation by Laughter", translated and performed by Bernstein. A co-composer is credited the same way, the music and performance of one piece being by Christopher Reiner "and included with permission", and the selection itself is signed "Selected by Charles Bernstein". The archive reads PennSound as a witness of a distinct type: a recording keeps the author's name, the performer's voice and a co-composer's credit as separate attributions, so that a reading of one poet's work by another collapses into neither, and its filing rule is the poet's name, with no evidence beyond the names it files under of whether a chosen name is kept as given. In the archive's account of heteronymy, ordinary translation, role-playing "understood as performance rather than as sustained authorial organization" and collaborative authorship that constitutes no distinct heteronym fall outside the concept, and a heteronymic architecture is said to make a collapse of plural functions register as loss; the census, for its part, tags PennSound as not limited to the poet's own voice.

Its holdings run from historic recordings by Ezra Pound, Wallace Stevens, Guillaume Apollinaire, William Carlos Williams and H.D. to what Wikipedia groups as more recent recordings, by Allen Ginsberg, John Ashbery, Jack Spicer, Gertrude Stein and Lyn Hejinian, with readings and sometimes musical versions of classical Greek poetry, Chaucer, Milton, Pope and Shakespeare; its historical selection opens with Apollinaire's "Le Pont Mirabeau" of 1913. A 2006 profile gave its emphasis as "the experimental and adventurous", across emerging and canonical poets, and the census gives its coverage as recordings from the 1910s onward, from the United States and elsewhere, with no geography stated. Its size is stated in two units: Wikipedia gives over 1500 full-length and single-poem recordings, "the largest collection of poetry sound-files on the internet", and in another sentence well over 50,000 sound files, while its Instagram account gives more than 50,000 recordings; its own saved site pages state no count.

Its recordings come from the poets themselves, from universities and institutions such as Harvard University's Woodberry Poetry Room, and from poets' estates, and it states the limit of its record: "We intend to provide as much documentation about individual recordings as possible; new bibliographic information will be added over time," with supplements invited. A 2006 profile reported the manifesto's commitment to recordings "with as much bibliographical and archival information as possible" and called the archive committed to dates and documentation for all of its recordings; the census counts complete bibliographic data for every recording among what the resource does not answer.

Its newest collection, announced on 27 March 2026, is a home for Charles Ruas's radio programming from the 1970s, 1980s and 2000s, launched with hundreds of recordings and "still under construction"; the Eric Mottram Centennial Collection is another. The PennSound Podcasts are produced by Al Filreis at the Kelly Writers House and listed on Jacket2, where episode 84, with Gina Myers, is dated 1 April 2026 and the editor, Hennessey, presents episodes of his own; his retrospective podcast, PennSound Rewind, received its own page in March 2026 and is published at PennSound and at Jacket2.org. With the Kelly Writers House and the Poetry Foundation it sponsors PoemTalk, a podcast discussing a different poet or poem each show. The census records it as active, with PennSound Daily posts from November 2025 to March 2026, and the newest listing on its home page is George Quasha reading genius foci at Barrytown, New York, on 14 July 2026.

Its files are free to stream and download as MP3s and are intended for non-commercial use by anyone, teachers and libraries included; the description on its YouTube channel states the terms in full: "All PennSound recordings are made available for noncommercial and educational use only; the featured writers and artists retain all copyrights to their work." The census, reading its site pages and its encyclopedia article, records the rights terms of individual recordings as not stated, counts who holds the rights to a recording among the questions the resource does not answer, and leaves any rights or permissions statement unchecked. A March 2026 post on its home page counts PennSound among "publicly funded distribution platforms" and presents the kind of programming that is lost when funding to the institutions that produce it is "suddenly cut for political reasons".

It works in collaboration with the Kelly Writers House, UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center, Jacket2, the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing and the University of Pennsylvania Libraries; its About page thanks UbuWeb and the Electronic Poetry Center, UbuWeb's creator Kenneth Goldsmith is among its senior editors, and the census enters UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center and Jacket2 as its neighbours.

Others describe it in their own terms: poets.org in 2006 as "a free online gallery, archive and radio show rolled into one"; ModPo, the site of a course in modern and contemporary American poetry, as "the largest archive of recordings of poets reading their own poems"; and its own X account, joined in March 2009, as an "audio & video archive of poetry & poetics" associated with the Kelly Writers House. On YouTube its channel has 2.16K subscribers and 338 videos; a one-minute video titled "Charles Bernstein - PennSound" is on The Brainwaves Video Anthology's channel, and two longer videos, of 51:52 on PennSound's channel and 54:21 on a channel named Jerry Inspired, carry no title beyond the platform's name.

The leesharks.com authorship census, which admits a resource that gathers and holds many works or records and says what it holds, enters PennSound as an empirical comparator in the areas of avant-garde and experimental archives and of attribution and credit, and asks of it how authored performance is recorded: whose voice a recording carries and under whose name it is filed, with performer and author credited apart. The census's anchors are the archive's paper on heteronymy and its essay on the existence tax, and its organizing question asks how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed. By the census's account the resource answers whether a recording of a named poet is held, who performs a recording where the performer differs from the author, and which reading series and events it has recorded, and it leaves unanswered how an author who writes under several names is filed; the census leaves the author pages, series pages and singles archive themselves to later reading, and Wikipedia's article, the field's encyclopedia source, was last edited on 22 September 2026.

Asked for the name on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview, at a new address, gave PennSound as "the world's largest free digital archive of poetry audio, featuring over 50,000 recordings spanning from 1913 to the present", with its host, its directors, its singles, its scope and its programs, and the Capture Registry found the host and the three directors exact and the Ruas collection carried, the 2005 launch left out. The registry traces the count to the Instagram card and Wikipedia's "Well over 50,000 sound files", and the year 1913 to Apollinaire's recording, and notes that the composition calls all the files recordings and names T.S. Eliot, who appears in none of the three PennSound pages the census saved. It found the separate credits absent: the composition files everything under author pages, "individual catalogs for thousands of writers", in keeping with the manifesto's rule of the poet's name, and has no place for a reading of one poet's work by another, the feature that makes PennSound a row of the census; the registry's analysis calls the archive composed accurately at its grain. The registry scored the composition's provenance at 0.25, the three directors and the Center named and the sources carded, and records PennSound as an external resource entered in the census on 1 November 2026 with its own pages saved by hash.

Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)PennSound

PennSound is an ongoing project of the University of Pennsylvania's Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing, producing new audio recordings of poets and preserving existing audio archives, free to stream and download; the archive reads it as a witness that credits author, performer and co-composer as separate attributions.

🎙️ What it holds

  • Filing: author, series, anthology and singles pages; readings cut into singles, complete readings kept.5↘
    It has been called the "iTunes for poetry", a phrase Wikipedia attributes to Charles Bernstein in an Associated Press article, and its running series of posts is PennSound Daily.§3 Recordings are filed on author pages, series pages, anthology, collection and group pages and in a singles archive, with Cinema, Classics, podcast and Close Listening collections and the PennSound Daily archive beside them.§7 Readings are broken down into singles, one poem to a file, and complete readings are also kept; a 2006 profile set this organization against "many poetry audio archives", and newly segmented readings, cut by poem and by topic, continue to be announced.§8 Its recordings come from the poets themselves, from universities and institutions such as Harvard University's Woodberry Poetry Room, and from poets' estates, and it states the limit of its record: "We intend to provide as much documentation about individual recordings as possible; new bibliographic information will be added over time," with supplements invited.§19 With the Kelly Writers House and the Poetry Foundation it sponsors PoemTalk, a podcast discussing a different poet or poem each show.§23
  • Credits: Clare performed by Bernstein; Weiner with Mattlin and Kraut; Khlebnikov translated and performed by Bernstein; music by Christopher Reiner, "included with permission".5↘
    PennSound is an ongoing project committed to producing new audio recordings and preserving existing audio archives: a poetry website and online archive that hosts free, downloadable recordings of poets reading their own work, and of others' work.§1 Where the reader differs from the author, a recording names both: the historical selection on the home page lists John Clare's "Vowelless Letter" (1849) performed by Charles Bernstein, Hannah Weiner's Clairvoyant Journal performed by Weiner, Sharon Mattlin and Rochelle Kraut, Kurt Schwitters's "Ur Sonata: Largo" performed by Ernst Schwitters (spelled "Scwhitter" on the page), and Velimir Khlebnikov's "Incantation by Laughter", translated and performed by Bernstein.§12 A co-composer is credited the same way, the music and performance of one piece being by Christopher Reiner "and included with permission", and the selection itself is signed "Selected by Charles Bernstein".§13 The archive reads PennSound as a witness of a distinct type: a recording keeps the author's name, the performer's voice and a co-composer's credit as separate attributions, so that a reading of one poet's work by another collapses into neither, and its filing rule is the poet's name, with no evidence beyond the names it files under of whether a chosen name is kept as given.§14 It found the separate credits absent: the composition files everything under author pages, "individual catalogs for thousands of writers", in keeping with the manifesto's rule of the poet's name, and has no place for a reading of one poet's work by another, the feature that makes PennSound a row of the census; the registry's analysis calls the archive composed accurately at its grain.§36
  • Scope: Apollinaire's 1913 recording to contemporary poets; Pound, Stevens, Stein, Hejinian; classics to Shakespeare.3↘
    Its holdings run from historic recordings by Ezra Pound, Wallace Stevens, Guillaume Apollinaire, William Carlos Williams and H.D. to what Wikipedia groups as more recent recordings, by Allen Ginsberg, John Ashbery, Jack Spicer, Gertrude Stein and Lyn Hejinian, with readings and sometimes musical versions of classical Greek poetry, Chaucer, Milton, Pope and Shakespeare; its historical selection opens with Apollinaire's "Le Pont Mirabeau" of 1913.§16 A 2006 profile gave its emphasis as "the experimental and adventurous", across emerging and canonical poets, and the census gives its coverage as recordings from the 1910s onward, from the United States and elsewhere, with no geography stated.§17 The registry traces the count to the Instagram card and Wikipedia's "Well over 50,000 sound files", and the year 1913 to Apollinaire's recording, and notes that the composition calls all the files recordings and names T.S. Eliot, who appears in none of the three PennSound pages the census saved.§35
  • Size: over 1500 recordings and well over 50,000 sound files (Wikipedia); "more than 50,000 recordings" (Instagram).3↘
    Its own YouTube channel calls it a Web-based archive for noncommercial distribution of the largest collection of poetry sound files on the Internet, and its Instagram account the world's preeminent online archive of poetry audio, with more than 50,000 recordings from 1913 to the present.§2 Its size is stated in two units: Wikipedia gives over 1500 full-length and single-poem recordings, "the largest collection of poetry sound-files on the internet", and in another sentence well over 50,000 sound files, while its Instagram account gives more than 50,000 recordings; its own saved site pages state no count.§18 The registry traces the count to the Instagram card and Wikipedia's "Well over 50,000 sound files", and the year 1913 to Apollinaire's recording, and notes that the composition calls all the files recordings and names T.S. Eliot, who appears in none of the three PennSound pages the census saved.§35

👥 Who runs it

  • Directors: Charles Bernstein, Al Filreis, Chris Mustazza; editor Michael S. Hennessey; two other descriptions list two directors.5↘
    It is a project of the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing at the University of Pennsylvania, whose site lists it among the Center's programs beside the Kelly Writers House events and ModPo, under the Center's director, Al Filreis; PennSound itself is directed by Charles Bernstein, Filreis and Chris Mustazza and edited by Michael S. Hennessey, with Danny Snelson and Kenneth Goldsmith as senior editors.§4 Two other descriptions name two directors: the description on its YouTube channel lists Bernstein and Filreis as directors, Hennessey as managing editor and Mark P. Lindsay as managing director, and a profile on poets.org, posted in December 2006, calls Bernstein one of the site's two directors along with Filreis.§5 The PennSound Podcasts are produced by Al Filreis at the Kelly Writers House and listed on Jacket2, where episode 84, with Gina Myers, is dated 1 April 2026 and the editor, Hennessey, presents episodes of his own; his retrospective podcast, PennSound Rewind, received its own page in March 2026 and is published at PennSound and at Jacket2.org.§22 It works in collaboration with the Kelly Writers House, UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center, Jacket2, the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing and the University of Pennsylvania Libraries; its About page thanks UbuWeb and the Electronic Poetry Center, UbuWeb's creator Kenneth Goldsmith is among its senior editors, and the census enters UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center and Jacket2 as its neighbours.§28 Asked for the name on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview, at a new address, gave PennSound as "the world's largest free digital archive of poetry audio, featuring over 50,000 recordings spanning from 1913 to the present", with its host, its directors, its singles, its scope and its programs, and the Capture Registry found the host and the three directors exact and the Ruas collection carried, the 2005 launch left out.§34
  • Founded: 2005, by Filreis and Bernstein; the "iTunes for poetry".4↘
    It has been called the "iTunes for poetry", a phrase Wikipedia attributes to Charles Bernstein in an Associated Press article, and its running series of posts is PennSound Daily.§3 Filreis and Bernstein created it, and it was launched in 2005; an article on Penn Today under the title "PennSound: All the Free Poetry You Care to Download" opens by setting it against a recording industry that "may not want anyone downloading music without paying for it".§6 Its files are free to stream and download as MP3s and are intended for non-commercial use by anyone, teachers and libraries included; the description on its YouTube channel states the terms in full: "All PennSound recordings are made available for noncommercial and educational use only; the featured writers and artists retain all copyrights to their work."§25 Asked for the name on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview, at a new address, gave PennSound as "the world's largest free digital archive of poetry audio, featuring over 50,000 recordings spanning from 1913 to the present", with its host, its directors, its singles, its scope and its programs, and the Capture Registry found the host and the three directors exact and the Ruas collection carried, the 2005 launch left out.§34

📜 Rules and terms

  • Manifesto: free, singles, every file named, retrievable "under the poet’s name".4↘
    The PennSound Manifesto, by Bernstein, sets six rules, among them that recordings be free and downloadable and broken down into singles, that all files be named, that bibliographic information be embedded in each file, and that sound files be indexed and retrievable from a library catalog under the poet's name and from search engines on the web; the About page links it and the launch press release.§9 The census records that a work is held under the poet's name on an author page and under a series name on series pages, such as Belladonna* and Love Jawns: A Mixtape, and that the saved pages state no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names.§10 The archive reads PennSound as a witness of a distinct type: a recording keeps the author's name, the performer's voice and a co-composer's credit as separate attributions, so that a reading of one poet's work by another collapses into neither, and its filing rule is the poet's name, with no evidence beyond the names it files under of whether a chosen name is kept as given.§14 It found the separate credits absent: the composition files everything under author pages, "individual catalogs for thousands of writers", in keeping with the manifesto's rule of the poet's name, and has no place for a reading of one poet's work by another, the feature that makes PennSound a row of the census; the registry's analysis calls the archive composed accurately at its grain.§36
  • Terms: noncommercial and educational use only; writers and artists keep all copyrights; rights per recording unstated in the census's sources.2↘
    Its files are free to stream and download as MP3s and are intended for non-commercial use by anyone, teachers and libraries included; the description on its YouTube channel states the terms in full: "All PennSound recordings are made available for noncommercial and educational use only; the featured writers and artists retain all copyrights to their work."§25 The census, reading its site pages and its encyclopedia article, records the rights terms of individual recordings as not stated, counts who holds the rights to a recording among the questions the resource does not answer, and leaves any rights or permissions statement unchecked.§26
  • Limits: documentation added over time; Ruas collection under construction.3↘
    Its recordings come from the poets themselves, from universities and institutions such as Harvard University's Woodberry Poetry Room, and from poets' estates, and it states the limit of its record: "We intend to provide as much documentation about individual recordings as possible; new bibliographic information will be added over time," with supplements invited.§19 A 2006 profile reported the manifesto's commitment to recordings "with as much bibliographical and archival information as possible" and called the archive committed to dates and documentation for all of its recordings; the census counts complete bibliographic data for every recording among what the resource does not answer.§20 Its newest collection, announced on 27 March 2026, is a home for Charles Ruas's radio programming from the 1970s, 1980s and 2000s, launched with hundreds of recordings and "still under construction"; the Eric Mottram Centennial Collection is another.§21

📻 Programs

  • Collections: Charles Ruas's radio programming (March 2026); Eric Mottram Centennial Collection.2↘
    Its newest collection, announced on 27 March 2026, is a home for Charles Ruas's radio programming from the 1970s, 1980s and 2000s, launched with hundreds of recordings and "still under construction"; the Eric Mottram Centennial Collection is another.§21 Asked for the name on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview, at a new address, gave PennSound as "the world's largest free digital archive of poetry audio, featuring over 50,000 recordings spanning from 1913 to the present", with its host, its directors, its singles, its scope and its programs, and the Capture Registry found the host and the three directors exact and the Ruas collection carried, the 2005 launch left out.§34
  • Podcasts: produced by Filreis at the Kelly Writers House; PennSound Rewind; PoemTalk with the Poetry Foundation.2↘
    The PennSound Podcasts are produced by Al Filreis at the Kelly Writers House and listed on Jacket2, where episode 84, with Gina Myers, is dated 1 April 2026 and the editor, Hennessey, presents episodes of his own; his retrospective podcast, PennSound Rewind, received its own page in March 2026 and is published at PennSound and at Jacket2.org.§22 With the Kelly Writers House and the Poetry Foundation it sponsors PoemTalk, a podcast discussing a different poet or poem each show.§23
  • Active: listings to July 2026; publicly funded.2↘
    The census records it as active, with PennSound Daily posts from November 2025 to March 2026, and the newest listing on its home page is George Quasha reading genius foci at Barrytown, New York, on 14 July 2026.§24 A March 2026 post on its home page counts PennSound among "publicly funded distribution platforms" and presents the kind of programming that is lost when funding to the institutions that produce it is "suddenly cut for political reasons".§27

🔗 Around it

  • Neighbours: Kelly Writers House, UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center, Jacket2.2↘
    The PennSound Podcasts are produced by Al Filreis at the Kelly Writers House and listed on Jacket2, where episode 84, with Gina Myers, is dated 1 April 2026 and the editor, Hennessey, presents episodes of his own; his retrospective podcast, PennSound Rewind, received its own page in March 2026 and is published at PennSound and at Jacket2.org.§22 It works in collaboration with the Kelly Writers House, UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center, Jacket2, the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing and the University of Pennsylvania Libraries; its About page thanks UbuWeb and the Electronic Poetry Center, UbuWeb's creator Kenneth Goldsmith is among its senior editors, and the census enters UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center and Jacket2 as its neighbours.§28
  • Elsewhere: poets.org, ModPo, X, YouTube.4↘
    Its own YouTube channel calls it a Web-based archive for noncommercial distribution of the largest collection of poetry sound files on the Internet, and its Instagram account the world's preeminent online archive of poetry audio, with more than 50,000 recordings from 1913 to the present.§2 Others describe it in their own terms: poets.org in 2006 as "a free online gallery, archive and radio show rolled into one"; ModPo, the site of a course in modern and contemporary American poetry, as "the largest archive of recordings of poets reading their own poems"; and its own X account, joined in March 2009, as an "audio & video archive of poetry & poetics" associated with the Kelly Writers House.§29 On YouTube its channel has 2.16K subscribers and 338 videos; a one-minute video titled "Charles Bernstein - PennSound" is on The Brainwaves Video Anthology's channel, and two longer videos, of 51:52 on PennSound's channel and 54:21 on a channel named Jerry Inspired, carry no title beyond the platform's name.§30 By the census's account the resource answers whether a recording of a named poet is held, who performs a recording where the performer differs from the author, and which reading series and events it has recorded, and it leaves unanswered how an author who writes under several names is filed; the census leaves the author pages, series pages and singles archive themselves to later reading, and Wikipedia's article, the field's encyclopedia source, was last edited on 22 September 2026.§33

📚 The archive's reading

  • Question: whose voice a recording carries and under whose name it is filed.2↘
    PennSound is an ongoing project committed to producing new audio recordings and preserving existing audio archives: a poetry website and online archive that hosts free, downloadable recordings of poets reading their own work, and of others' work.§1 The leesharks.com authorship census, which admits a resource that gathers and holds many works or records and says what it holds, enters PennSound as an empirical comparator in the areas of avant-garde and experimental archives and of attribution and credit, and asks of it how authored performance is recorded: whose voice a recording carries and under whose name it is filed, with performer and author credited apart.§31
  • Heteronymy: the civil name as attribution's unit; performance, translation and collaboration outside heteronymy; collapse as loss (#940).3↘
    The archive's paper on heteronymy holds that a civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across the systems that govern scholarly, literary, institutional and platform production, copyright among them, and it distinguishes the pseudonym, which changes the label attached to an authorial function, from the heteronym, which changes the organization of the function itself.§11 In the archive's account of heteronymy, ordinary translation, role-playing "understood as performance rather than as sustained authorial organization" and collaborative authorship that constitutes no distinct heteronym fall outside the concept, and a heteronymic architecture is said to make a collapse of plural functions register as loss; the census, for its part, tags PennSound as not limited to the poet's own voice.§15 The census's anchors are the archive's paper on heteronymy and its essay on the existence tax, and its organizing question asks how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed.§32
  • Unanswered: rights; full bibliography; an author with several names.4↘
    In the archive's account of heteronymy, ordinary translation, role-playing "understood as performance rather than as sustained authorial organization" and collaborative authorship that constitutes no distinct heteronym fall outside the concept, and a heteronymic architecture is said to make a collapse of plural functions register as loss; the census, for its part, tags PennSound as not limited to the poet's own voice.§15 A 2006 profile reported the manifesto's commitment to recordings "with as much bibliographical and archival information as possible" and called the archive committed to dates and documentation for all of its recordings; the census counts complete bibliographic data for every recording among what the resource does not answer.§20 The census, reading its site pages and its encyclopedia article, records the rights terms of individual recordings as not stated, counts who holds the rights to a recording among the questions the resource does not answer, and leaves any rights or permissions statement unchecked.§26 By the census's account the resource answers whether a recording of a named poet is held, who performs a recording where the performer differs from the author, and which reading series and events it has recorded, and it leaves unanswered how an author who writes under several names is filed; the census leaves the author pages, series pages and singles archive themselves to later reading, and Wikipedia's article, the field's encyclopedia source, was last edited on 22 September 2026.§33

[QUERENT] PennSound

[SYSTEM] [PennSound](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXAHrOzAViuA3Bb-ryGiQsu9iGuJgHNnG5WkQ2UgcoVHsWm9po_1c2DpsRRcxQIzDtfa0-l8pJXFLqNNHqgNjYpsOEW1hRjeFkBc5_26JQndUzdySDKfcdRC8BoRX) is the world's largest free digital archive of poetry audio, featuring over 50,000 recordings spanning from 1913 to the present. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXwHrOzAVqw-UL9Z3DzIo9LN9uX05R0Cbcmj80blqRglty7MWZk2yIMgmiJlfs5v-yQ7q-9vsdjwvUMNTDCTK8pFsp3gyh4C57_hYz_5da0XquFMnJSscuLZf_5cqkNoq), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXAHrOzAVH0ikNxz1kR0rHwsNCi5tGBgETURJR7ej4Em4lZ89BVvSDREVxjLWVyyNh_Prxe7XKTU6dVVgOGZmprHvQkB5kQ99jjIcswkqva5gQfPGVT_KoenMu68U)]
Overview & Mission

* Host & Location: Based at the University of Pennsylvania's Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing (CPCW) and associated with the [Kelly Writers House](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESUgHrOzAVr8uUV5erVkfAVbOIkt_HVL3Up84WQN9vwxjtmjBbov1j_HnxN4uWPrt6wtISDGkGukw1FCER9nw2EnVW9YrBwEXLPGR9eimpxfzQiPE). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESTwHrOzAVltkE_lW1mx6eejYsMiZVJZ0rKA7Hq8hDrDtr_TmSGvQ8iQrlPB5md1RslxqnspV6g_4rUYhNI34qJ0oq9O6IUWsrq1g-jRzIOqE), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXwHrOzAVqw-UL9Z3DzIo9LN9uX05R0Cbcmj80blqRglty7MWZk2yIMgmiJlfs5v-yQ7q-9vsdjwvUMNTDCTK8pFsp3gyh4C57_hYz_5da0XquFMnJSscuLZf_5cqkNoq)]
* Directors: Co-directed by Al Filreis, Charles Bernstein, and Chris Mustazza. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXwHrOzAVqw-UL9Z3DzIo9LN9uX05R0Cbcmj80blqRglty7MWZk2yIMgmiJlfs5v-yQ7q-9vsdjwvUMNTDCTK8pFsp3gyh4C57_hYz_5da0XquFMnJSscuLZf_5cqkNoq)]
* Format: Emphasizes individual poem "singles" rather than just full-length readings, making files easy to stream and download as MP3s for free. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWAHrOzAVLvqGRzeZL34BJ98RVjge0UCXcpTeuCWKVB7umrjMv3Fc1PcLentKXFfhcSsTzTpDlAA0bgcIctSi-d2X1XQPqE6g7gkUAmCnCIlhXgpPPB7-WQY), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEShAEB6zswFeqLwQDlMl4KL47Pqgcvbr0KacULWztoV4NYgi6fTJmssq2gBKac3YEokPIMpQeGzrHB9gkZzpSS0qthCJo6lUm4BjsDsGCOJanZP2iqtzBy98yhKJYA1mP46vxX8cUHBarlgfxjeQ8a51GK3-UruFgpf06lqMexfr7oSHIThTg)]
* Scope: Includes early canonical and modernist voices (such as William Carlos Williams, Wallace Stevens, Gertrude Stein, and T.S. Eliot) alongside contemporary, experimental, and international poets. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAV16_iHR6kpCYhyRowlctvZ1OmDF56gZrNjLV5yvymSIj9w17kX1G4BTDHSpev0bFFDeAjjiCAua6VDNOlxh3etgHJ6XSkEQ_eKKV1koKLCH7DGC1LprB6em8kARBDSR8ngvSi), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYwHrOzAV2PbBJDYYjVl4-bHiksGOs0Zhvas3WiaUPp67Pd8HNF8I8cLSduA8h9u5kovkrWSGMDPLDupcx5zaK6hWia-d9jmtHKCje9VKtf5uPmG021Ut3u2kUDctG6xuAtBSKQ)]

Key Features & Programs

* Author Pages: Extensive, individual catalogs for thousands of writers, including recent additions like the [Charles Ruas Author Page](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXAHrOzAViuA3Bb-ryGiQsu9iGuJgHNnG5WkQ2UgcoVHsWm9po_1c2DpsRRcxQIzDtfa0-l8pJXFLqNNHqgNjYpsOEW1hRjeFkBc5_26JQndUzdySDKfcdRC8BoRX) featuring historical radio interviews. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXAHrOzAViuA3Bb-ryGiQsu9iGuJgHNnG5WkQ2UgcoVHsWm9po_1c2DpsRRcxQIzDtfa0-l8pJXFLqNNHqgNjYpsOEW1hRjeFkBc5_26JQndUzdySDKfcdRC8BoRX), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXQHrOzAVJaCwBAImGTgyfqB-pG1RmuDhApcfGEkvZuyA1_Km9fFugEUaOpx6r-aC_IMZG3tWuPT1HC5e-X7oM8vxgSTq5ODvSXu39L01Ba_f5iWz2SWoXwKriBGyiw)]
* PennSound Podcasts: Regular audio programming produced at the Kelly Writers House, including series like PennSound Rewind hosted by Michael Hennessey. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVgHrOzAVCNk06QnuW6TsYqfO2zWQnUCsGNnr4sg0VnPaIwLz9oFxZNLGGm39TcuucB7vBH6xLkFw3FTX19V8yAHSKCwfQYu4Jgwh_yWokfCZ-n8p8Gur), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXAHrOzAViuA3Bb-ryGiQsu9iGuJgHNnG5WkQ2UgcoVHsWm9po_1c2DpsRRcxQIzDtfa0-l8pJXFLqNNHqgNjYpsOEW1hRjeFkBc5_26JQndUzdySDKfcdRC8BoRX)]
* PoemTalk: A co-produced podcast series (with Jacket2) featuring roundtable discussions on individual poems from the archive. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYwHrOzAVP7XHdT7Kcv3S2FuxEG0P1g7iBYPV3kMmNun-D-KPKLeADEZFQSwO4p0MJgTlh00h2XKaHBp6oYcSoFkOYYXt_MmTH7uxu2K-rllfpceIsNwOSrvY-u78UrpCJUbISw), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVgHrOzAVCNk06QnuW6TsYqfO2zWQnUCsGNnr4sg0VnPaIwLz9oFxZNLGGm39TcuucB7vBH6xLkFw3FTX19V8yAHSKCwfQYu4Jgwh_yWokfCZ-n8p8Gur)]
* Archive Access: All audio files are open-access and noncommercial. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWQHrOzAVNuKKmLMdOsdQZOW-AKyz-7T43Qn5nsnSYxoBSuISOWqtboHNGGzx8N-hHLWU9K-_ch7xV82Bt49XE1lmEt86PJkvmW4Vi7tKOUMbiqiwFlnseJ5D), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXwHrOzAVqw-UL9Z3DzIo9LN9uX05R0Cbcmj80blqRglty7MWZk2yIMgmiJlfs5v-yQ7q-9vsdjwvUMNTDCTK8pFsp3gyh4C57_hYz_5da0XquFMnJSscuLZf_5cqkNoq)]

PennSound

PennSound is an ongoing project committed to producing new audio recordings and preserving existing audio archives, and is described as a poetry website and online archive that hosts free and downloadable recordings of poets reading their own work. On YouTube PennSound describes itself as a Web-based archive for noncommercial distribution of the largest collection of poetry sound files on the Internet; on Instagram, as the world's preeminent online archive of poetry audio, more than 50,000 recordings from 1913 to the present. Bernstein called it the "iTunes for poetry" in an Associated Press article, as Wikipedia reports, and every recording is a free downloadable MP3.

It is a project of the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing, which lists it with the Kelly Writers House events and ModPo under its director, Al Filreis; PennSound is directed by Charles Bernstein, Al Filreis and Chris Mustazza, with Michael S. Hennessey as editor and Danny Snelson and Kenneth Goldsmith as senior editors. The YouTube channel's description lists two directors, Bernstein and Filreis, with Hennessey as managing editor and Mark P. Lindsay as managing director, and poets.org's 2006 profile called Bernstein one of the site's two directors. Created by Filreis and Bernstein, it launched in 2005; a Penn Today article titled "PennSound: All the Free Poetry You Care to Download" opens on the recording industry.

Recordings sit on author pages, series pages, anthology, collection and group pages and in a singles archive, with Cinema, Classics, Close Listening and the PennSound Daily archive. Readings are broken down into singles, with complete readings available, and newly segmented readings are announced on ModPo; poets.org set the singles against many poetry audio archives. Its manifesto, by Bernstein, requires free downloadable recordings in singles, named files, embedded bibliographic information, and indexing under the poet's name in a library catalog and in web search; the About page links it and the launch press release.

The historical selection credits performers beside authors: Clare's "Vowelless Letter" performed by Bernstein, Weiner's Clairvoyant Journal performed by Weiner, Mattlin and Kraut, Schwitters's "Ur Sonata" performed by Ernst Schwitters, and Khlebnikov translated and performed by Bernstein; one piece's music and performance are by Christopher Reiner, included with permission, and the selection is signed by Bernstein.

Its holdings include historic recordings by Pound, Stevens, Apollinaire, Williams and H.D., more recent ones by Ginsberg, Ashbery, Spicer, Stein and Hejinian, and classics from Greek poetry to Shakespeare, from Apollinaire's 1913 "Le Pont Mirabeau"; poets.org gave its emphasis as the experimental and adventurous. Wikipedia gives over 1500 full-length and single-poem recordings and well over 50,000 sound files.

Recordings come from poets, institutions such as the Woodberry Poetry Room, and estates; documentation is added over time, as its About page states, and poets.org reported a commitment to dates and documentation for every recording.

The Charles Ruas collection of radio programming launched on 27 March 2026 with hundreds of recordings and is still under construction; PennSound Rewind, Hennessey's retrospective podcast, got its own page that March, and the newest listing is of 14 July 2026. The PennSound Podcasts are produced by Filreis at the Kelly Writers House and listed on Jacket2, the newest being episode 84 of 1 April 2026, some presented by Hennessey; PoemTalk is sponsored with the Kelly Writers House and the Poetry Foundation.

The files are for non-commercial use, by teachers and libraries among others, and the YouTube channel adds that the recordings are for noncommercial and educational use only and that the writers and artists retain all copyrights. A March 2026 post calls PennSound a publicly funded distribution platform and names programming lost when funding is cut for political reasons.

It collaborates with the Kelly Writers House, UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center, Jacket2, the Center and the Penn Libraries, and thanks UbuWeb and the Electronic Poetry Center.

poets.org called it a free online gallery, archive and radio show; ModPo, the largest archive of recordings of poets reading their own poems; its X account, joined in 2009, an audio and video archive of poetry and poetics associated with the Kelly Writers House. Its YouTube channel has 2.16K subscribers and 338 videos, and three video cards stand beside it, one titled "Charles Bernstein - PennSound"; its Wikipedia article was last edited on 22 September 2026.

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)PennSound

PennSound is an ongoing project of the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing at the University of Pennsylvania, producing new audio recordings and preserving audio archives of poetry, free to stream and download.

🎙️ Holdings

  • Filing: author, series, anthology and singles pages; singles and complete readings.3↘
    Recordings sit on author pages, series pages, anthology, collection and group pages and in a singles archive, with Cinema, Classics, Close Listening and the PennSound Daily archive.§7 Readings are broken down into singles, with complete readings available, and newly segmented readings are announced on ModPo; poets.org set the singles against many poetry audio archives.§8 Recordings come from poets, institutions such as the Woodberry Poetry Room, and estates; documentation is added over time, as its About page states, and poets.org reported a commitment to dates and documentation for every recording.§13
  • Credits: performers named beside authors; a co-composer "included with permission".1↘
    The historical selection credits performers beside authors: Clare's "Vowelless Letter" performed by Bernstein, Weiner's Clairvoyant Journal performed by Weiner, Mattlin and Kraut, Schwitters's "Ur Sonata" performed by Ernst Schwitters, and Khlebnikov translated and performed by Bernstein; one piece's music and performance are by Christopher Reiner, included with permission, and the selection is signed by Bernstein.§10
  • Scope and size: from 1913; over 1500 recordings, 50,000 sound files.3↘
    On YouTube PennSound describes itself as a Web-based archive for noncommercial distribution of the largest collection of poetry sound files on the Internet; on Instagram, as the world's preeminent online archive of poetry audio, more than 50,000 recordings from 1913 to the present.§2 Its holdings include historic recordings by Pound, Stevens, Apollinaire, Williams and H.D., more recent ones by Ginsberg, Ashbery, Spicer, Stein and Hejinian, and classics from Greek poetry to Shakespeare, from Apollinaire's 1913 "Le Pont Mirabeau"; poets.org gave its emphasis as the experimental and adventurous.§11 Wikipedia gives over 1500 full-length and single-poem recordings and well over 50,000 sound files.§12

👥 People and terms

  • Directors: Bernstein, Filreis, Mustazza; editor Hennessey; launched 2005.5↘
    Bernstein called it the "iTunes for poetry" in an Associated Press article, as Wikipedia reports, and every recording is a free downloadable MP3.§3 It is a project of the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing, which lists it with the Kelly Writers House events and ModPo under its director, Al Filreis; PennSound is directed by Charles Bernstein, Al Filreis and Chris Mustazza, with Michael S. Hennessey as editor and Danny Snelson and Kenneth Goldsmith as senior editors.§4 The YouTube channel's description lists two directors, Bernstein and Filreis, with Hennessey as managing editor and Mark P. Lindsay as managing director, and poets.org's 2006 profile called Bernstein one of the site's two directors.§5 Created by Filreis and Bernstein, it launched in 2005; a Penn Today article titled "PennSound: All the Free Poetry You Care to Download" opens on the recording industry.§6 The PennSound Podcasts are produced by Filreis at the Kelly Writers House and listed on Jacket2, the newest being episode 84 of 1 April 2026, some presented by Hennessey; PoemTalk is sponsored with the Kelly Writers House and the Poetry Foundation.§15
  • Manifesto: named files, retrievable under the poet's name.1↘
    Its manifesto, by Bernstein, requires free downloadable recordings in singles, named files, embedded bibliographic information, and indexing under the poet's name in a library catalog and in web search; the About page links it and the launch press release.§9
  • Terms: noncommercial and educational use; copyrights retained by writers and artists.1↘
    The files are for non-commercial use, by teachers and libraries among others, and the YouTube channel adds that the recordings are for noncommercial and educational use only and that the writers and artists retain all copyrights.§16
  • Limits: documentation added over time.2↘
    Recordings come from poets, institutions such as the Woodberry Poetry Room, and estates; documentation is added over time, as its About page states, and poets.org reported a commitment to dates and documentation for every recording.§13 The Charles Ruas collection of radio programming launched on 27 March 2026 with hundreds of recordings and is still under construction; PennSound Rewind, Hennessey's retrospective podcast, got its own page that March, and the newest listing is of 14 July 2026.§14

📻 Programs and neighbours

  • Programs: the Ruas collection, podcasts, PennSound Rewind, PoemTalk; publicly funded.3↘
    The Charles Ruas collection of radio programming launched on 27 March 2026 with hundreds of recordings and is still under construction; PennSound Rewind, Hennessey's retrospective podcast, got its own page that March, and the newest listing is of 14 July 2026.§14 The PennSound Podcasts are produced by Filreis at the Kelly Writers House and listed on Jacket2, the newest being episode 84 of 1 April 2026, some presented by Hennessey; PoemTalk is sponsored with the Kelly Writers House and the Poetry Foundation.§15 A March 2026 post calls PennSound a publicly funded distribution platform and names programming lost when funding is cut for political reasons.§17
  • Around it: Kelly Writers House, UbuWeb, the EPC, Jacket2; poets.org, ModPo, X, YouTube.4↘
    On YouTube PennSound describes itself as a Web-based archive for noncommercial distribution of the largest collection of poetry sound files on the Internet; on Instagram, as the world's preeminent online archive of poetry audio, more than 50,000 recordings from 1913 to the present.§2 It collaborates with the Kelly Writers House, UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center, Jacket2, the Center and the Penn Libraries, and thanks UbuWeb and the Electronic Poetry Center.§18 poets.org called it a free online gallery, archive and radio show; ModPo, the largest archive of recordings of poets reading their own poems; its X account, joined in 2009, an audio and video archive of poetry and poetics associated with the Kelly Writers House.§19 Its YouTube channel has 2.16K subscribers and 338 videos, and three video cards stand beside it, one titled "Charles Bernstein - PennSound"; its Wikipedia article was last edited on 22 September 2026.§20

PennSound is an ongoing project committed to producing new audio recordings and preserving existing audio archives, and is described as a poetry website and online archive that hosts free and downloadable recordings of poets reading their own work. On YouTube PennSound describes itself as a Web-based archive for noncommercial distribution of the largest collection of poetry sound files on the Internet; on Instagram, as the world's preeminent online archive of poetry audio, more than 50,000 recordings from 1913 to the present. Bernstein called it the "iTunes for poetry" in an Associated Press article, as Wikipedia reports, and every recording is a free downloadable MP3. It is a project of the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing, which lists it with the Kelly Writers House events and ModPo under its director, Al Filreis; PennSound is directed by Charles Bernstein, Al Filreis and Chris Mustazza, with Michael S. Hennessey as editor and Danny Snelson and Kenneth Goldsmith as senior editors. The YouTube channel's description lists two directors, Bernstein and Filreis, with Hennessey as managing editor and Mark P. Lindsay as managing director, and poets.org's 2006 profile called Bernstein one of the site's two directors. Created by Filreis and Bernstein, it launched in 2005; a Penn Today article titled "PennSound: All the Free Poetry You Care to Download" opens on the recording industry. Recordings sit on author pages, series pages, anthology, collection and group pages and in a singles archive, with Cinema, Classics, Close Listening and the PennSound Daily archive. Readings are broken down into singles, with complete readings available, and newly segmented readings are announced on ModPo; poets.org set the singles against many poetry audio archives. Its manifesto, by Bernstein, requires free downloadable recordings in singles, named files, embedded bibliographic information, and indexing under the poet's name in a library catalog and in web search; the About page links it and the launch press release. The historical selection credits performers beside authors: Clare's "Vowelless Letter" performed by Bernstein, Weiner's Clairvoyant Journal performed by Weiner, Mattlin and Kraut, Schwitters's "Ur Sonata" performed by Ernst Schwitters, and Khlebnikov translated and performed by Bernstein; one piece's music and performance are by Christopher Reiner, included with permission, and the selection is signed by Bernstein. Its holdings include historic recordings by Pound, Stevens, Apollinaire, Williams and H.D., more recent ones by Ginsberg, Ashbery, Spicer, Stein and Hejinian, and classics from Greek poetry to Shakespeare, from Apollinaire's 1913 "Le Pont Mirabeau"; poets.org gave its emphasis as the experimental and adventurous. Wikipedia gives over 1500 full-length and single-poem recordings and well over 50,000 sound files. Recordings come from poets, institutions such as the Woodberry Poetry Room, and estates; documentation is added over time, as its About page states, and poets.org reported a commitment to dates and documentation for every recording. The Charles Ruas collection of radio programming launched on 27 March 2026 with hundreds of recordings and is still under construction; PennSound Rewind, Hennessey's retrospective podcast, got its own page that March, and the newest listing is of 14 July 2026. The PennSound Podcasts are produced by Filreis at the Kelly Writers House and listed on Jacket2, the newest being episode 84 of 1 April 2026, some presented by Hennessey; PoemTalk is sponsored with the Kelly Writers House and the Poetry Foundation. The files are for non-commercial use, by teachers and libraries among others, and the YouTube channel adds that the recordings are for noncommercial and educational use only and that the writers and artists retain all copyrights. A March 2026 post calls PennSound a publicly funded distribution platform and names programming lost when funding is cut for political reasons. It collaborates with the Kelly Writers House, UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center, Jacket2, the Center and the Penn Libraries, and thanks UbuWeb and the Electronic Poetry Center. poets.org called it a free online gallery, archive and radio show; ModPo, the largest archive of recordings of poets reading their own poems; its X account, joined in 2009, an audio and video archive of poetry and poetics associated with the Kelly Writers House. Its YouTube channel has 2.16K subscribers and 338 videos, and three video cards stand beside it, one titled "Charles Bernstein - PennSound"; its Wikipedia article was last edited on 22 September 2026.

PennSound is an ongoing project committed to producing new audio recordings and preserving existing audio archives: a poetry website and online archive that hosts free, downloadable recordings of poets reading their own work, and of others' work. Its own YouTube channel calls it a Web-based archive for noncommercial distribution of the largest collection of poetry sound files on the Internet, and its Instagram account the world's preeminent online archive of poetry audio, with more than 50,000 recordings from 1913 to the present. It has been called the "iTunes for poetry", a phrase Wikipedia attributes to Charles Bernstein in an Associated Press article, and its running series of posts is PennSound Daily. It is a project of the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing at the University of Pennsylvania, whose site lists it among the Center's programs beside the Kelly Writers House events and ModPo, under the Center's director, Al Filreis; PennSound itself is directed by Charles Bernstein, Filreis and Chris Mustazza and edited by Michael S. Hennessey, with Danny Snelson and Kenneth Goldsmith as senior editors. Two other descriptions name two directors: the description on its YouTube channel lists Bernstein and Filreis as directors, Hennessey as managing editor and Mark P. Lindsay as managing director, and a profile on poets.org, posted in December 2006, calls Bernstein one of the site's two directors along with Filreis. Filreis and Bernstein created it, and it was launched in 2005; an article on Penn Today under the title "PennSound: All the Free Poetry You Care to Download" opens by setting it against a recording industry that "may not want anyone downloading music without paying for it". Recordings are filed on author pages, series pages, anthology, collection and group pages and in a singles archive, with Cinema, Classics, podcast and Close Listening collections and the PennSound Daily archive beside them. Readings are broken down into singles, one poem to a file, and complete readings are also kept; a 2006 profile set this organization against "many poetry audio archives", and newly segmented readings, cut by poem and by topic, continue to be announced. The PennSound Manifesto, by Bernstein, sets six rules, among them that recordings be free and downloadable and broken down into singles, that all files be named, that bibliographic information be embedded in each file, and that sound files be indexed and retrievable from a library catalog under the poet's name and from search engines on the web; the About page links it and the launch press release. The census records that a work is held under the poet's name on an author page and under a series name on series pages, such as Belladonna* and Love Jawns: A Mixtape, and that the saved pages state no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names. The archive's paper on heteronymy holds that a civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across the systems that govern scholarly, literary, institutional and platform production, copyright among them, and it distinguishes the pseudonym, which changes the label attached to an authorial function, from the heteronym, which changes the organization of the function itself. Where the reader differs from the author, a recording names both: the historical selection on the home page lists John Clare's "Vowelless Letter" (1849) performed by Charles Bernstein, Hannah Weiner's Clairvoyant Journal performed by Weiner, Sharon Mattlin and Rochelle Kraut, Kurt Schwitters's "Ur Sonata: Largo" performed by Ernst Schwitters (spelled "Scwhitter" on the page), and Velimir Khlebnikov's "Incantation by Laughter", translated and performed by Bernstein. A co-composer is credited the same way, the music and performance of one piece being by Christopher Reiner "and included with permission", and the selection itself is signed "Selected by Charles Bernstein". The archive reads PennSound as a witness of a distinct type: a recording keeps the author's name, the performer's voice and a co-composer's credit as separate attributions, so that a reading of one poet's work by another collapses into neither, and its filing rule is the poet's name, with no evidence beyond the names it files under of whether a chosen name is kept as given. In the archive's account of heteronymy, ordinary translation, role-playing "understood as performance rather than as sustained authorial organization" and collaborative authorship that constitutes no distinct heteronym fall outside the concept, and a heteronymic architecture is said to make a collapse of plural functions register as loss; the census, for its part, tags PennSound as not limited to the poet's own voice. Its holdings run from historic recordings by Ezra Pound, Wallace Stevens, Guillaume Apollinaire, William Carlos Williams and H.D. to what Wikipedia groups as more recent recordings, by Allen Ginsberg, John Ashbery, Jack Spicer, Gertrude Stein and Lyn Hejinian, with readings and sometimes musical versions of classical Greek poetry, Chaucer, Milton, Pope and Shakespeare; its historical selection opens with Apollinaire's "Le Pont Mirabeau" of 1913. A 2006 profile gave its emphasis as "the experimental and adventurous", across emerging and canonical poets, and the census gives its coverage as recordings from the 1910s onward, from the United States and elsewhere, with no geography stated. Its size is stated in two units: Wikipedia gives over 1500 full-length and single-poem recordings, "the largest collection of poetry sound-files on the internet", and in another sentence well over 50,000 sound files, while its Instagram account gives more than 50,000 recordings; its own saved site pages state no count. Its recordings come from the poets themselves, from universities and institutions such as Harvard University's Woodberry Poetry Room, and from poets' estates, and it states the limit of its record: "We intend to provide as much documentation about individual recordings as possible; new bibliographic information will be added over time," with supplements invited. A 2006 profile reported the manifesto's commitment to recordings "with as much bibliographical and archival information as possible" and called the archive committed to dates and documentation for all of its recordings; the census counts complete bibliographic data for every recording among what the resource does not answer. Its newest collection, announced on 27 March 2026, is a home for Charles Ruas's radio programming from the 1970s, 1980s and 2000s, launched with hundreds of recordings and "still under construction"; the Eric Mottram Centennial Collection is another. The PennSound Podcasts are produced by Al Filreis at the Kelly Writers House and listed on Jacket2, where episode 84, with Gina Myers, is dated 1 April 2026 and the editor, Hennessey, presents episodes of his own; his retrospective podcast, PennSound Rewind, received its own page in March 2026 and is published at PennSound and at Jacket2.org. With the Kelly Writers House and the Poetry Foundation it sponsors PoemTalk, a podcast discussing a different poet or poem each show. The census records it as active, with PennSound Daily posts from November 2025 to March 2026, and the newest listing on its home page is George Quasha reading genius foci at Barrytown, New York, on 14 July 2026. Its files are free to stream and download as MP3s and are intended for non-commercial use by anyone, teachers and libraries included; the description on its YouTube channel states the terms in full: "All PennSound recordings are made available for noncommercial and educational use only; the featured writers and artists retain all copyrights to their work." The census, reading its site pages and its encyclopedia article, records the rights terms of individual recordings as not stated, counts who holds the rights to a recording among the questions the resource does not answer, and leaves any rights or permissions statement unchecked. A March 2026 post on its home page counts PennSound among "publicly funded distribution platforms" and presents the kind of programming that is lost when funding to the institutions that produce it is "suddenly cut for political reasons". It works in collaboration with the Kelly Writers House, UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center, Jacket2, the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing and the University of Pennsylvania Libraries; its About page thanks UbuWeb and the Electronic Poetry Center, UbuWeb's creator Kenneth Goldsmith is among its senior editors, and the census enters UbuWeb, the Electronic Poetry Center and Jacket2 as its neighbours. Others describe it in their own terms: poets.org in 2006 as "a free online gallery, archive and radio show rolled into one"; ModPo, the site of a course in modern and contemporary American poetry, as "the largest archive of recordings of poets reading their own poems"; and its own X account, joined in March 2009, as an "audio & video archive of poetry & poetics" associated with the Kelly Writers House. On YouTube its channel has 2.16K subscribers and 338 videos; a one-minute video titled "Charles Bernstein - PennSound" is on The Brainwaves Video Anthology's channel, and two longer videos, of 51:52 on PennSound's channel and 54:21 on a channel named Jerry Inspired, carry no title beyond the platform's name. The leesharks.com authorship census, which admits a resource that gathers and holds many works or records and says what it holds, enters PennSound as an empirical comparator in the areas of avant-garde and experimental archives and of attribution and credit, and asks of it how authored performance is recorded: whose voice a recording carries and under whose name it is filed, with performer and author credited apart. The census's anchors are the archive's paper on heteronymy and its essay on the existence tax, and its organizing question asks how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed. By the census's account the resource answers whether a recording of a named poet is held, who performs a recording where the performer differs from the author, and which reading series and events it has recorded, and it leaves unanswered how an author who writes under several names is filed; the census leaves the author pages, series pages and singles archive themselves to later reading, and Wikipedia's article, the field's encyclopedia source, was last edited on 22 September 2026. Asked for the name on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview, at a new address, gave PennSound as "the world's largest free digital archive of poetry audio, featuring over 50,000 recordings spanning from 1913 to the present", with its host, its directors, its singles, its scope and its programs, and the Capture Registry found the host and the three directors exact and the Ruas collection carried, the 2005 launch left out. The registry traces the count to the Instagram card and Wikipedia's "Well over 50,000 sound files", and the year 1913 to Apollinaire's recording, and notes that the composition calls all the files recordings and names T.S. Eliot, who appears in none of the three PennSound pages the census saved. It found the separate credits absent: the composition files everything under author pages, "individual catalogs for thousands of writers", in keeping with the manifesto's rule of the poet's name, and has no place for a reading of one poet's work by another, the feature that makes PennSound a row of the census; the registry's analysis calls the archive composed accurately at its grain. The registry scored the composition's provenance at 0.25, the three directors and the Center named and the sources carded, and records PennSound as an external resource entered in the census on 1 November 2026 with its own pages saved by hash.
